newsitem.title: UK: S&P says Portuguese banks still vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: S&P says Portuguese banks still vulnerable.

text.p: Standard & Poors said on Monday the Portuguese banking system had been deregulated without creating major stresses in the banks' financial profiles.

But the heightened competition meant the "continuing downward trend" in the profitability of Portuguese banks and their relatively low level of commission income, made them more vulnerable to a decline in the net interest margin.
"The worry that this margin will continue to slide is one reason why Portuguese ratings are not higher than they are," said Yves Burger in a statement from S&P.

S&P said Burger underlined the contrast between the present system, dominated by a handful of "mainly private sector banks....subject to the same broad body of regulations as other European banks" and the situation in the mid-1980s, when it was "more fragmented, almost entirely state-owned, closed to fresh competition, and subject to regulations that limited banks' product range and segmented the market between commercial, savings, and investment banks."

The agency said although deregulation had also sparked a credit boom that led to a fairly deep recession in 1993-1994 and a consequent drop in asset quality, the Portuguese financial system "did not suffer serious stress, in contrast with many other systems that have been deregulated."
Burger suggested possible reasons for this were because credit expansion was less powerful than it might have been and because the Portuguese authorities never lost monetary policy credibility.

S&P said Burger detected "the emergence of more dynamic commercial approaches among the privatised banks since...first contact with Portuguese banks in 1991." This had been spurred largely by aggressive newcomers such as Banco Comercial Portugues and Banco Portugues de Investimento.

"These two banks have contributed significantly to the rapid consolidation of the banking system since the beginning of this decade. Five banking groups now account for 82 percent of all banking assets -an exceptionally high level of concentration for Europe," S&P said.

S&P said Burger noted "little evidence of the financial excess that has often been associated with deregulation in other countries." But he did suggest that the full impact of many reforms had yet to be felt and that, consequently, "the next two to three years will be critical ones for Portuguese banking."
